title: How to Get More Google Reviews for Your Business
description: How contractors get more Google reviews: a simple ask system, texts you can copy today, and the Google rules you must not break.

takeaways: Ask every customer, right after the final walk, and send your direct review link by text. One tap beats a search every time.

body:
You get more Google reviews by asking every customer once, at the end of the job, with a direct link they can tap. Most happy clients never leave a review for one plain reason: nobody asked, or they had to hunt for your listing. Fix those two things, stay inside Google rules, and reviews become a steady habit instead of a lucky streak.

## The rules first: what Google bans

Get this part wrong and the reviews you collect can be removed. Google treats these as fake engagement and rating manipulation on its official policy pages.

| Practice | Allowed? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ask every customer for an honest review | Yes | Google allows asking for reviews of a real experience |
| Send your review link or QR code | Yes | Google gives you both inside your Business Profile |
| Pay, discount or give a gift for a review | No | Google bans incentives for posting, changing or removing a review |
| Ask only customers you expect to praise you | No | Google bans selectively asking for positive reviews, called review gating |
| Have staff, family or friends post reviews | No | Conflict of interest, and not a real customer experience |
| Hand the client your phone and wait while they type | No | Google bans pressuring people to review while on the premises |
| Set staff review quotas or ask for your name in reviews | No | Google lists both as rating manipulation |

Google own help page on reviews puts it plainly: offering incentives, like free or discounted goods or services, in exchange for a review, a changed review or a removed negative review is strictly prohibited. US law backs this up. The FTC consumer review rule, in force since October 21, 2024, bans buying reviews tied to a set sentiment and bans fake reviews, and it lets courts set civil penalties for knowing violations. Ask everyone, offer nothing, script nothing. That is the whole legal line, and it is easy to stay inside it. If your profile itself needs work first, start with our [Google Business Profile guide for contractors](/blog/google-business-profile-for-contractors/).

## Your review system in four steps

**Step 1: Get your link.** Open your Business Profile, choose Read reviews, then Get more reviews. Copy the short link and save the QR code. Google notes the QR code is made on a computer browser, not on a phone, so set this up once at a desk. Test the link on your own phone before you send it to anyone.

**Step 2: Ask at the final walk.** Stand in the finished room, confirm the client is happy with the work, then ask in person. Follow it with a text within the hour, while the job is still fresh. A request sent two weeks later competes with everything else in their inbox.

**Step 3: Put the link where clients already look.** Add it to your final invoice, your email signature, your thank-you email and a small printed card you leave behind with the QR code on it. One link, many doors.

**Step 4: Reply and track.** Reply to every review, good or bad, within a few days. Once a week, count asks sent and reviews posted. That ratio tells you if the system is running or just planned.

## Worked example: one month of painting jobs

Say your crew finishes 20 jobs in a month. You ask all 20 clients in person and send all 20 the text below the same day. This is a planning example with round numbers, so you can run it with your own figures.

- Asks sent: 20
- If 8 of 20 clients post a review, that is a 40 percent response (8 / 20)
- Reviews gained that month: 8
- Over 6 months at the same pace: 8 x 6 = 48 new reviews

Check the math the other way: 48 reviews over 6 months, at 20 jobs a month, is 48 out of 120 clients, again 40 percent. If your real response is lower, the fix is almost never a new tool. It is asking sooner, asking in person first, and making the link one tap. Track your own response rate for a month before you change anything, so you know your true starting point.

## Texts and scripts you can use today

Copy these as they are. Fill in the name, the job and your link. None of them asks for five stars, and none offers anything in return. That is on purpose.

**In person, at the final walk:**
"If you are happy with how this turned out, a Google review helps a small crew like ours a lot. I will text you our link so it takes under a minute."

**Text, sent the same day:**
"Hi [Name], thanks for having us paint your [kitchen]. If you have a minute, we would value your honest review here: [review link]. Thanks again, [Your name], [Business name]."

**Email, with the final invoice:**
"Thanks for choosing [Business name] for your [job]. If you would like to share how it went, here is our Google review link: [review link]. Honest words help the next homeowner in [town] pick a painter with confidence."

**One reminder, 4 to 5 days later, only if no review yet:**
"Hi [Name], a quick nudge on that review link from last week: [review link]. No pressure at all if you are busy. Thanks for the work."

**Checklist for every finished job:**
- Final walk done and client confirms they are happy with the work
- Verbal ask made in person
- Text with review link sent within 1 hour
- Link also on the final invoice and thank-you email
- Reminder set for day 4 or 5, one time only
- Reply posted to every new review within 3 days

## How to reply to reviews

Keep replies short, personal and calm. For a good review, thank them by name and name the job: "Thanks, Sarah. Glad the cabinet color landed well." For a bad review, do not argue in public. Thank them, say sorry for the part that went wrong, and invite them to call you so you can fix it. Every future client reads that reply as a sample of how you handle problems. If a review is fake, from a person you never worked for, flag it inside your profile for Google to check instead of trading words with it. Reviews that break Google content rules are the ones Google can remove. An honest low rating from a real client stays, and a string of good reviews is the honest way past it.

Ask at the same point on every job and this stops depending on memory. The crews with 100-plus reviews are not luckier. They just ask every time. Pair the habit with the basics in our [contractor website checklist](/blog/contractor-website-checklist/), and read how the same review engine feeds new work in our guide to [painting business leads](/blog/painting-business-leads/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I offer a discount for a Google review?
No. Google bans any incentive, including discounts, gift cards, free extras or prize entries, for posting, changing or removing a review. Reviews posted for an incentive count as fake engagement and can be removed, and your profile can face limits.

### Is it against the rules to ask only happy customers?
Yes. Sending the review link only to clients you expect to praise you, and sending unhappy clients to a private form instead, is review gating. Google bans selectively asking for positive reviews. Ask every customer the same way.

### When is the best time to ask for a review?
At the final walk, the same day the job ends, with a text link sent within the hour. Send one reminder 4 to 5 days later if they have not posted. After that, stop. More reminders feel like pressure.

### How do I find my Google review link?
Open your Business Profile on a computer, choose Read reviews, then Get more reviews. Copy the short link and save the QR code from the same screen. Test the link on your phone before you send it out.

### Should I reply to negative reviews?
Yes, once, in public, and keep it short. Thank the client, own the part that went wrong, and give a phone number to sort it out. Do not offer anything in trade for changing the review. That offer itself breaks Google rules.

## Next step
Set up your review link today, print the QR card, and add the ask to your final walk on the next job you finish.
